claims.text: Retention of a single-phase solid solution is governed by the balance between configurational entropy and the mixing enthalpy of the constituent metals.
High configurational entropy raises barriers to atomic diffusion and rearrangement.
When the barrier to atomic rearrangement exceeds the available thermal activation energy, nanoparticles maintain a uniform, well-mixed structure.
Five-or-more-metal nanoparticles in near-equal atomic ratios can initially form a crystallized single-phase solid solution.
The proposed stabilization mechanism maintains structural and chemical stability throughout 473–1923 K.
Configurational-entropy-associated sluggish diffusion results in a uniform elemental distribution after annealing.
A moderate, not strongly exothermic, mixing enthalpy contributes to maintenance of the single-phase solid solution.
Entropy-induced diffusion barriers prevent phase segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Large atomic-size mismatch can overcome entropy stabilization and cause secondary-phase formation.
Unfavorable mixing enthalpy can overcome entropy stabilization and cause secondary-phase formation.
Nanoparticles with sufficiently high computationally predicted mixing barriers and entropy stabilization will retain their solid-solution structure under operating conditions.
Retention of the solid solution will be observed as an XRD pattern with no additional diffraction peaks.
Structurally stable nanoparticles will maintain both catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles that lack the proposed stabilization conditions will exhibit phase separation or elemental segregation.
The hypothesis applies preferentially to nanoparticles with balanced atomic radii.
Exceptionally exothermic mixing enthalpy can lower the effective diffusion barrier and promote segregation.
Slow cooling permits the effects of configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy on diffusion kinetics to be observed.
